Mosaic Law
moh-ZAY-ik LAW
noun phrase
English compound of Mosaic (of or pertaining to Moses; from Latin Mosaeus, from Hebrew Mosheh, possibly Egyptian ms, “son,” or Hebrew for “drawn out,” Exod. 2:10) + law (Old English lagu, from Old Norse lög, that which is laid down, a fixed rule); the compound denotes the body of divine legislation given through Moses at Sinai, codified in Exodus through Deuteronomy; distinguished by Reformed theologians into three categories: moral law (the Decalogue), ceremonial law (sacrificial and ritual ordinances), and civil law (Israel's national governance code).

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The Mosaic Law is the covenant legislation God gave to Israel through Moses at Sinai, constituting the legal foundation of the Old Covenant community. Reformed exegetes organize its 613 traditional commandments into three categories serving distinct redemptive-historical purposes. The moral law—summarized in the Ten Commandments (Exod. 20:1–17; Deut. 5:6–21)—is the perpetual expression of God's own character and the standard binding on all mankind in every age. The ceremonial law—sacrifices, feast days, Levitical cleansings, priesthood regulations—pointed typologically to Christ and was fulfilled and therefore abrogated in His atoning work (Col. 2:16–17; Heb. 10:1–18). The civil law—penalties, land regulations, national governance—applied the moral law to Israel's theocratic condition; its general equity remains instructive for civil order while its particular statutes do not bind Gentile nations.

The tripartite distinction guards against two errors: antinomian confusion that collapses all law with the ceremonial, and moralistic confusion that binds Israel's civil penalties on modern states. The apostle Paul describes the Mosaic law as “our tutor to lead us to Christ” (Gal. 3:24)—its function was to make sin's gravity visible, drive the conscience to the Savior, and foreshadow His redemptive work. Christ did not abolish the law but fulfilled it (Matt. 5:17); the Spirit now writes the moral law on the regenerate heart (Jer. 31:33; Heb. 8:10), completing under grace what Sinai began under covenant.

Origin & Era

The compound “Mosaic Law” is a modern scholarly designation; the Westminster Confession (19.3–5) codified the classic tripartite distinction into moral, ceremonial, and judicial (civil) law that the Reformed tradition has employed for four centuries.

expand to see more

Westminster Confession 19.2: “This law...he delivered to Israel in the Ten Commandments”—identifying the Decalogue as the permanent moral core of the Mosaic legislation, binding on all men in every age as an expression of God's unchanging character.

Westminster Confession 19.3: “Beside this law, commonly called moral, God was pleased to give to the people of Israel, as a church under age, ceremonial laws, containing several typical ordinances...all which ceremonial laws are now abrogated under the new testament.”

Westminster Confession 19.4: “To them also, as a body politic, he gave sundry judicial laws, which expired together with the state of that people...not obliging any other now, further than the general equity thereof may require.”

John Calvin (Institutes IV.20.14) on the judicial laws: “Equity alone must be the goal and rule and limit of all laws...all laws may justly be condemned which confound this distinction between political constitutions and the moral law.”

The 1689 LBCF (19.3–4) follows Westminster closely on the tripartite division, affirming the moral law as perpetually binding, the ceremonial law as abrogated in Christ, and the judicial law as expired with the Israelite polity but instructive in its general equity.

Key Scripture

John 1:17 — "The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ."

Rom. 10:4 — "For Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness — to everyone who believes."

Gal. 3:24 — "Therefore the Law has become our tutor to lead us to Christ — so that we may be justified by faith."

Matt. 5:17 — "Do not think that I came to abolish the Law or the Prophets. I did not come to abolish — but to fulfill."

Modern Corruption

Antinomians abolish the tripartite distinction and dismiss all law as obsolete under grace, while theonomists bind Israel's civil penalties on modern states—both errors collapsing the distinctions the Reformed tradition carefully maintains.

expand to see more

Antinomianism (from its 16th-century Lutheran form through its contemporary hyper-grace expression) collapses the ceremonial abolition into a general abolition of the law, producing Christians who treat the moral law as irrelevant to the sanctified life. The New Testament directly refutes this: Paul upholds the law for the unrighteous (1 Tim. 1:9), confirms the law is holy and spiritual (Rom. 7:12, 14), and teaches that the Spirit's work is to write the moral law on the regenerate heart (Rom. 8:4). The Reformers were precise: the ceremonial law is abolished as a type fulfilled; the moral law is confirmed as an expression of the character of God who does not change.

At the opposite error, theonomy (Rushdoony, Bahnsen) argues that the Mosaic civil law—including its specific penalties (death for adultery, Sabbath-breaking, etc.)—is normative for modern civil governments. The Westminster Confession's “general equity” clause (19.4) allows the civil law's underlying principles to inform public ethics; it does not extend to binding modern states to Israel's theocratic code, which expired with that particular national polity. The civil law was Israel's constitution as a covenant nation with a specific redemptive-historical role; post-Calvary, that role has been fulfilled and the constitution has expired, though its general moral equity remains instructive.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Rooted in the Hebrew Torah (instruction, direction), the divine body of legislation given at Sinai and organized in the Reformed tradition into its three distinct categories according to their redemptive-historical purposes.

expand to see more

Hebrew Torah (תורה) — instruction, direction, teaching; from yarah (to instruct, to direct, to shoot); the primary Hebrew designation for the Mosaic legislation, covering not just legal statutes but narrative, covenant history, and prophetic wisdom

Hebrew choq / mishpat / mitzvah — the three main categories of Old Testament legal language: choq (statute, fixed rule), mishpat (judgment, case-law ruling), mitzvah (commandment, direct divine directive); together they form the texture of the Mosaic code

Greek nomos (νόμος) — law; the LXX and New Testament term for the Mosaic legislation; Paul's extended treatment in Galatians and Romans unpacks the law's relationship to promise, faith, and fulfillment in Christ

Latin lex mosaica — the Scholastic and Reformed designation for the Mosaic body of law; the tripartite division (moral/ceremonial/civil) was systematized by Aquinas and adopted—with Reformed modifications—in the Westminster and 1689 confessions

Sinai covenant — the specific historical occasion (Exod. 19–24; Deut. 5) at which God gave the Mosaic legislation to Israel; distinguishable from the Abrahamic and Davidic covenants in its national and typological functions, yet unified with them in the one covenant of grace

Usage

"The Westminster Confession's tripartite distinction—moral, ceremonial, civil—is not a medieval Catholic imposition but a careful exegetical recovery of the New Testament's own categories: ceremonial law abolished (Col. 2:16-17), moral law confirmed (Rom. 7:12; 8:4), civil law expired but instructive in its equity."

"When Jesus says “I did not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it” (Matt. 5:17), He is affirming the moral law as the standard His active obedience satisfies and His Spirit writes on regenerate hearts—not abrogating it, and not extending Israel's civil penalties to Gentile nations."

"Paul's “tutor” metaphor (Gal. 3:24) captures the law's pedagogical function: it drove Israel to the end of its own righteousness so that the Messiah's righteousness would be received as the only ground of standing before God."
